lesson.title: Running Out of Room: What Happens When Recursion Never Stops
lesson.summary: A stack overflow happens when recursive calls pile up faster than they return, exhausting the memory set aside for the call stack, and Python protects against it by raising a RecursionError before your program crashes.
lesson.body:
The recursive call stack chapter showed that every recursive call pushes a new frame, and that frame stays in memory until its call returns. If a function keeps calling itself without ever reaching a base case, or reaches one only after an enormous number of calls, frames keep piling up with nothing coming off the top. Eventually there is no more room to push another frame, a condition called a stack overflow. This is precisely the failure mode that a correctly written base case exists to prevent.

Here is a function with no base case at all:

def count_up(n):
    return count_up(n + 1)

count_up(0)

Trace: count_up(0) calls count_up(1), which calls count_up(2), which calls count_up(3), and so on, with no condition anywhere that stops the calls or returns a value directly. Rather than letting this run until the operating system itself runs out of memory, which is what would eventually happen in a language like C, Python keeps a built in limit on how many frames the call stack is allowed to hold. When that limit is exceeded, Python raises RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded, instead of crashing silently or corrupting memory.

That limit is a real, inspectable number. Calling import sys and then sys.getrecursionlimit() returns Python's current limit, which defaults to 1000 in a standard CPython installation. You can change it with sys.setrecursionlimit(3000), but raising the limit does not fix a missing or unreachable base case, it just delays the RecursionError and increases the chance of a genuine, lower level crash if the underlying system stack also runs out first, since Python's limit is a safety check layered on top of the operating system's own, smaller stack.

Because RecursionError is an ordinary Python exception, it can be caught with try and except like any other error, which distinguishes it from a true operating system level stack overflow in languages without that safety net. That said, catching a RecursionError should be treated as an emergency fallback, not a design strategy: the correct fix for count_up is not a bigger recursion limit or a try block, it is a real base case, some condition, for example n >= 1000000, that returns instead of recursing again.

It is worth being precise about the difference between a bug that merely produces a wrong answer and one that produces a stack overflow. A recursive case with a broken base case condition, one that is never actually reached, for example checking n == 0 on a function whose recursive step always adds a fixed amount larger than what would land exactly on zero, will keep recursing forever, silently consuming the entire call stack before Python has any chance to detect the mistake early. Tracing your base case reachability by hand, the same way you would trace countdown(3) or sum_list, is the cheapest way to catch this before it turns into a RecursionError at runtime.
